Small animal silhouettes fill stacked bands, while fine teeth form a narrow fringe at the bottom.
Three shallow curved bays interrupt the upper edge. Long narrow teeth turn the lower half into parallel lines.
Thin incised horizontal lines divide a broad strip above a short surviving row of teeth; the top edge has rounded bays.
A broad rounded disc balances over a narrow handle, with outward branches filling the transition between them.
A rounded metal disc sits above a fan-shaped junction and a long wooden handle marked by narrow vertical grooves.
The photograph shows the metal disc detached from a pale handle. The handle widens into a curved supporting end.
A turquoise grid runs across the top of a long dark box. Small playing pieces introduce compact upright forms beside it.
Closely spaced horizontal coils climb a rounded wall that narrows toward the upper edge.
Concentric rounds organise a domed lid, while repeated stitched units break the outer wall into small intervals.
Wide upright strips structure a small rounded container. A thicker reddish binding gathers the upper edge.
Blue-green and warm bands interrupt the horizontal weave; small stepped blocks turn the surface into a patterned field. Detached fragments are shown nearby.
Bent arms and legs organise the figure around a small working area. A rectangular field of objects occupies the right side.
Light vertical bars fill the back of a dark wooden chair. The seat forms a pale plane above separated legs.
Carved figures and signs fill a rectangular wooden panel, with vertical divisions and irregular broken edges.
A row of openwork forms fills the upper back. The broad woven seat contrasts with the narrow upright frame and curved legs.
A tall panelled back rises above a densely woven seat. The front legs narrow and curve near the floor.
A shallow woven seat stretches between four short supports, joined by low horizontal braces.
The stool combines a worn upper surface with curved upright supports and long horizontal feet.
Two diagonal frames cross to make an X-shaped structure. Long top rails contrast with small shaped feet.
An upward-curving cradle rests above several narrow struts and an oval base.
A shallow crescent sits on a single narrow stem that flares toward a broad foot.
The central support widens smoothly into a broad base beneath an upward-curving cradle. A dark band interrupts the stem.
A long thin wooden body contains recesses and contrasting dark and reddish fields, with slender reeds beside it.
A small projecting head joins a broad flattened body, turning the entire stone slab into an animal-like outline.
A rounded fish-shaped body narrows into a tail. Tiny notches and drilled openings interrupt the otherwise simple outline.
Horizontal bands climb a long neck, while looped petal-like outlines follow the rounded shoulder and body.
The plain rounded wall rises toward a broad elliptical opening. Cracks interrupt the surface but not the overall volume.
Two rounded volumes meet at a narrowed waist beneath a small neck. Dark vertical marks contrast with the blue glaze.
A small outward rim caps a short neck, a broad shoulder, and a gently narrowing lower body.
A wide open bowl has gently curving sides that narrow toward a small supporting foot. The supplied image is monochrome.
Warm translucent-looking stone bands pass through a rounded bowl and thick rim.
Pale vertical streaks cross the rounded wall of a stone bowl. The wide opening reveals its interior. A display support is visible below.
A circular hollow joins a projecting sign-like form and raised arm shapes on a flat stone field.
A very shallow dish forms a long ellipse in the photograph; a fine speckled surface softens its plain profile.
Repeated light and blue scallops wrap a dark vessel with a narrow neck, small handles, and a foot.
Two short handles create openings beside a narrow neck above a nearly spherical dark body.
Blue-and-light edging emphasises the rim, handles, and foot against a broad warm-coloured body.
A black upper zone meets a long reddish body with a narrow base. The boundary is softer than the outer contour.
The cup narrows at its middle and flares at the rim and foot. Small inscribed fields occupy the outward-facing wall.
A nearly cylindrical blue-green cup has a thickened lip and small changes in surface tone.
Several long dark marks sit in a pale rounded fragment with an uneven outer border.
A small round rosette adjoins a striped curved field. Broken edges reveal that this is only part of a larger decoration.
Fine scalloped bands cover a long neck and rounded lower body; large missing areas interrupt the vessel wall.
A broad pale wall slopes toward a small flat base, with a subtle horizontal division below the rim.
Fine parallel pleats run across separate surviving textile fragments. Irregular tears contrast with the repeated folds.

guides/hieroglyphs-how-to-look.html.title: Hieroglyphs - how to look
guides/hieroglyphs-how-to-look.html.description:
Open the ancient working drawingHieroglyphic writing records language. Signs may represent sounds, words, or help indicate a word's category. It is not a one-picture-to-one-English-letter alphabet. The role of a sign depends on its use in a text.Start by observing direction, grouping, proportion, and spacing. Human and animal signs generally face the beginning of a line; read towards their faces. Horizontal lines can run in either direction, while columns normally run from top to bottom. For an actual reading or translation, use a scholarly transcription and the complete context.Signs are arranged into visually balanced groups. Tall, broad, and small forms fit together rather than occupying identical modern letter boxes. The ruled working drawing above is a reference for planning and scaling, not an instruction to make all Egyptian text a rigid grid.
Limestone working drawing — contours and construction lines.
Heqanakht's letter — hieratic handwriting, a different script appearance.
Scarab seal field — signs fitted into an oval.
Shabti of Seti I — text running over a three-dimensional figure. For formal inspiration, study spacing and proportion while labelling the result as a modern composition. If you use an actual inscription, preserve its orientation and source; changing, mirroring, or rearranging signs can change or destroy its reading. This vault does not provide automatic name translations.
Sources: Bibliotheca Alexandrina, The Hieroglyphic Writing and Arrangement and Direction of Writing. Object details are linked in the individual notes.

studio/seven-studies-to-begin.html.title: Seven studies to begin
studio/seven-studies-to-begin.html.description:
Proportion: draw the sign grid and study occupied versus empty cells.
Silhouette: compare the faience ankh and wooden ankh at thumbnail size.
Repetition: draw the outer envelope of the falcon's wings, then add feather groups.
Plant geometry: turn the lotus inlay into a study of interlocking coloured planes.
Curved rhythm: compare Wah's collar with Hapiankhtifi's collar.
Composition: map the inscription and figure areas in the offering niche. Your own work: combine one spacing rule, one contour rule, and one material palette. Write down which references informed each choice. Keep actual inscriptions intact or use your own text.
Duplicate Templates/Study template to record a sketch. Make a source study first, then put your own invention on a separate page.

studio/build-a-motif-sheet.html.title: Build a motif sheet
studio/build-a-motif-sheet.html.description: Use Indexes/Visual vocabulary and Indexes/Materials to select three objects with a related visual feature and different materials. Make one thumbnail of each complete object before isolating details. Draw six small units: two contours, two borders, and two empty spaces. Label every unit with its reference link. Record the operation behind each unit: mirror, alternate, stack, turn, frame, taper, or interlock. Make a row of eight units. Change only spacing first, then scale, then orientation. Compare the three rows. Apply the most useful rule to your own plant, animal, or abstract shape. Keep inscriptions as documented source studies. Decorative-looking signs may be writing; do not describe an invented arrangement as a translation.Finish with three notes: which rule survived the change of subject, which relied on the original material, and which needs more source research.

studio/from-flat-pattern-to-volume.html.title: From flat pattern to volume
studio/from-flat-pattern-to-volume.html.description:
Start in Collections/Vessels and surface patterns or Collections/Everyday objects and making.Draw a vessel profile, then make a paper cylinder with similar proportions. Divide the surface into rim, body, and base. On a flat strip, test a border with one repeated unit and a larger quiet field. Wrap the strip around the cylinder and photograph the seam.Compare the flat and wrapped versions. Which shapes compress at the edges? Where does the pattern begin and end? Is a handle an interruption or part of the rhythm? Draw the negative space of the opening separately.
Make a second version with an invented motif. Record the source, the borrowed compositional rule, and your changes using Templates/Study template.

studio/three-passes-through-an-object.ht.title: Three passes through an object
studio/three-passes-through-an-object.ht.description: Choose an image · Record your studyChoose one object. Draw its outside edge at three sizes without surface detail. Mark holes as shapes. Write which proportion makes the object recognisable; do not substitute a generic Egyptian motif for what is actually visible.On a second drawing, mark the centre line, supports, joins, divisions, and repeated units. Separate surviving ancient material from a museum reconstruction when the source identifies one. Draw hidden parts only as an explicitly labelled proposal.Map colour and ornament on top of the structural drawing. Compare a smooth area with a dense area. Identify where a motif bends around a volume or stops at a border.Transfer one formal rule to a new subject: a repeating interval, a ratio, a framed field, or a contrast of surfaces. Keep the source study and invented design on separate pages. Link the reference and note what changed.

info_attractionForce.description: How much should linked nodes attract each other? This will make the graph appear more clustered.

info_linkLength.description: How long should the links between nodes be? The shorter the links the more connected nodes will cluster together.

info_repulsionForce.description: How much should nodes repel each other? This will make disconnected parts more spread out.

info_centralForce.description: How much should nodes be attracted to the center? This will make the graph appear more dense and circular.

info_edgePruning.description: Edges with a length above this threshold will not be rendered, however they will still contribute to the simulation. This can help large tangled graphs look more organised. Hovering over a node will still display these links.

info_minNodeRadius.description: How small should the smallest nodes be? The smaller a node is the less it will attract other nodes.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.
